title: GenScale: A Benchmark for Relative Object Scale in Image Generation and Editing
claim: State-of-the-art generators and editors violate real-world relative object sizes across tasks, while our post-hoc method yields plausible scale.
layout: Task-row by model-column grid; condition left, baselines then ours rightmost; dashed divider
description: A grid of photographic samples organized by task. Rows are grouped into Task 1 (text-to-image generation, with scenarios S1 natural depth and S2 same plane), Task 2 (image-conditioned generation, S3 reference plus dimensions) and Task 3 (editing, S4 auto-discovery and S5 shrink). The left column, in tinted rounded boxes (blue, pink, green), gives the prompt or input condition, such as banana plus bicycle or a frisbee and watch error image. A dashed vertical line separates it from six output columns: GPT Image 2, Nano Banana 2, Qwen Image/Edit, FLUX.2 Kontext, SD 3.5 Large (+IP), and ReScale (Ours) in bold on the far right. Baselines show objects at wrong relative sizes, such as a giant banana, a huge frisbee or a tiny laptop. The Ours column shows plausible proportions. Rotated labels on the right edge name the task types.

abstract: Modern image generation and editing systems can produce photorealistic, prompt-aligned images, but still often render familiar objects at implausible relative sizes. To measure this failure mode, we introduce GenScale, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for real-world relative object scale in image generation and editing. GenScale contains 900 image-level entries and 1,643 pairwise anchor-target scale relations across common-object generation, human-product generation with metric dimensions, and scale correction from failed generations. We further design a human-calibrated ordinal judge for scalable pairwise scale evaluation. Last but not least, we introduce Rescale, a model-agnostic post-processing agent for localized scale correction without modifying the source generator. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art image generators and editors do not reliably render plausible relative scale, while Rescale consistently improves scale plausibility across generated and edited images. Together, GenScale establishes relative object scale as a distinct, measurable, and actionable capability for image generation systems.
